content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the tests for reducing sugars, non-reducing sugars, starch, proteins, and lipids
Explain the science behind each test

are simple chemical tests used to identify biological molecules in food samples. Each test produces a characteristic colour change that indicates the presence of a specific type of molecule. These tests are fundamental practical skills in biology.
Add 2 cm³ of Benedict's solution to 2 cm³ of sample
Heat in water bath at 80°C for 5 minutes
First test with Benedict's (should be negative)
Heat in water bath to hydrolyse
If now positive = non-reducing sugar was present
Benedict's doesn't work in acid conditions
Must return to neutral/slightly alkaline pH
Add few drops of iodine solution to sample
Iodine molecules fit inside amylose helix
Add 2 cm³ of sample to test tube
Add 2 cm³ of dilute NaOH (sodium hydroxide)
Add few drops of dilute CuSO₄ (copper sulfate) solution
Cu²⁺ ions form complex with peptide bonds
Add NaOH first, then copper sulfate
Don't add too much copper sulfate
Add sample to 2 cm³ of ethanol
Add the ethanol solution to 2 cm³ of water
When added to water, lipids come out of solution
Droplets scatter light → appears cloudy white
Can use colorimeter for accurate measurement
Compare to standards of known concentration
If negative, test for non-reducing sugars
Benedict's test works on all sugars
Blue-black colour in iodine test means it's negative
It's blue; it turns purple when protein present
Sugar that can donate electrons (reduce Cu²⁺)
Sugar that cannot reduce Benedict's directly
Copper sulfate solution for testing sugars
Benedict's test: reducing sugars turn blue → orange/brick red (heat required)
Non-reducing sugars: hydrolyse first with acid, then Benedict's
Iodine test: starch turns yellow-brown → blue-black (no heat)
Biuret test: proteins turn blue → purple (no heat)
Emulsion test: lipids form cloudy white layer (no heat)
